MASTER COOPER

MASTER’S REPORT ON FAMILY PROPERTY
ACCOUNTING

[
1
]

This is a reference to the master for an accounting under
The
Family Property Act
pursuant to an order made by Allen J. on July 30, 2007.

The Reference Order

[
2
]

The reference order is contained in a twenty-six page final order
pronounced by Allen J.  It is not a standard reference for an accounting under
s. 15 of
The Family Property Act.

The specific terms are
as follows:

12.0 THIS COURT
ORDERS AND DECLARES pursuant to
The Family Property Act
that:

12.1    The
property agreement (pre-nuptial agreement) signed by the parties hereto on August
15, 1995 is a spousal agreement within the meaning of Section 1(1) of
The
Family Property Act
, having met all of the requirements of this section and
this agreement is valid and binding on MICHAEL KALO and on DAFNA BRENLEE
SHORE-KALO;

12.2.   DAFNA
BRENLEE SHORE-KALO’S interest in the Dafna trust and in its predecessor the
Dafna Shore Trust and in any and all of the underlying assets of these Trusts
is not shareable under
The Family Property Act
and shall not form any
part of an accounting before the Master of this Court;

12.3.   MICHAEL
KALO’S claim against DAFNA BRENLEE SHORE-KALO for $175,000.00 under
The
Family Property Act
is hereby dismissed and shall not form any part of an
accounting before the Master of this Court;

12.4.   The
funds standing in the joint bank account of the parties at the date of their
separation have already been equally divided between the parties and shall not
form any part of an accounting before the Master of this Court or form part of
any further proceedings before this Court;

12.5.   MICHAEL
KALO’S claim to a division of the remaining joint property of the parties
(one-half of the wedding presents received by the parties that were retained by
DAFNA BRENLEE SHORE-KALO on the date the parties separated and to one half of
the jointly acquired household possessions of the parties that were in the
marital home as at the date of their separation) shall be referred to the
Master of this Court for determination;

12.6.   That
portion of the DAFNA BRENLEE SHORE-KALO’S pension that she had with her Israeli
employer Radview Software that was accrued between the date of marriage of the
parties and the date of their separation shall be divided equally and this
matter is referred to a Master of this Court for determination, which
determination shall take into account only the contributions made by DAFNA
BRENLEE SHORE-KALO from the date of the marriage of the parties to the date of
their separation and in this process the Master shall determine whether there
were any pre-marriage contributions to this pension and if so how much;

12.7.   Upon
the Master determining the shareable portion of this pension, DAFNA BRENLEE
SHORE-KALO shall make a payment to MICHAEL KALO equal to the cash equivalent of
one half of the shareable portion of same;

12.8.   For
the purpose of any inquiries made by the Master pursuant to this Order, the
date of separation of the parties is found to be March 9, 2003 and the date of
marriage of the parties is found to be August 20, 1995;

12.9.   With
the exception of the matters referred to the Master for determination as set
out above, the remaining claims of MICHAEL KALO pursuant to
The

Family
Property Act
and for a division and sharing of assets and family property
are hereby dismissed.

[
3
]

The Queen’s Bench Rules applicable to the reference are found in
two parts of the rules: Part XIII References and Rule 70 Family Proceedings.
Part XIII contains the following rules
inter alia
:

Reference
of whole proceeding or issue

54.02(1)    Subject
to any right to have an issue tried by a jury, a judge may at any time in a
proceeding direct a reference of the whole proceeding or a reference to
determine an issue where,

(a) all
affected parties consent;

(b) a
prolonged examination of documents or an investigation is required that, in the
opinion of the judge, cannot conveniently be made at trial; or

(c) a
substantial issue in dispute requires the taking of accounts.

.
. .

54.04(1)    An
order directing a reference

(a) shall

(i) specify
the nature and subject matter of the reference,

(ii) designate
which party is to have carriage of the reference, and

(iii) …;
and

(b) may

(i) direct
in general terms that all necessary inquiries be made, accounts taken and costs
assessed, and

(ii) contain
directions for the conduct of the reference.

.
. .

[
4
]

Rule 70.25 applies specifically to references under
The
Family Property Act
.
The rule provides in part:

Family Property Act references

70.25(1)    This
rule applies to a reference before a master for an accounting of assets and
liabilities between spouses or common-law partners under section 15 of
The
Family Property Act
or for any other matter under
The Family Property
Act
directed by a judge for a reference before a master.

Order of reference

70.25(2)    An
order directing a reference to a master for an accounting of assets and
liabilities pursuant to section 15 of
The Family Property Act
shall set
out the valuation date determined in accordance with section 16 of that Act
unless the issue of determining the valuation date is specifically referred to
the master in the order.

Directions
from judge re shareability issues

70.25(3)    If
issues of shareability of assets or liabilities or ownership of assets are to
be determined on the reference, directions shall be set out in the order of
reference to delegate the determination of these issues to the master as part
of the scope of the reference.

Directions from judge re non-shareable assets or debts

70.25(4)    If
jointly held assets or liabilities, or other assets or liabilities, alleged to
be excluded from the application of
The Family Property Act
are to be
valued on a reference, a specific direction for the valuation of such assets or
liabilities shall be set out in the order of reference.

…

Rules 54 and 55 apply

70.25(12)   Part XIII
of the Rules (references) applies to a reference before the master under this
rule.

[
5
]

The order did not specify which party was to have conduct of the
reference. In family property act references, this is not unusual as Rule 70
provides a special procedure for these references which allows either party to
initiate the reference.  In this instance, the respondent initiated the
reference and the documents required by Rule 70 were filed by the parties
although they are not really applicable in this case given they are designed for
a section 15 accounting rather than the specific reference that was directed
here.

[
6
]

Justice Allen’s order directs the master to determine the
following three issues only:

1.
The respondent’s claim to one half of the wedding presents received by the
parties that were retained by the petitioner on the date the parties separated.

2.
The respondent’s claim to one half of the jointly acquired household
possessions of the parties that were in the marital home as at the date of
their separation.

3.
The respondent’s claim to that portion of the petitioner’s pension with her
Israeli employer Radview Software that was accrued between the date of the
marriage of the parties and the date of their separation.

First Hearing for Directions November 6, 2007

[
7
]

I was assigned to preside over the first hearing for directions
in accordance
with the Winnipeg
masters’ practice on references in family proceedings. The masters’ court has a
two–stage process for family property act accountings. The first stage - the
preliminary hearing(s) before a master – has essentially two purposes: to
explore possibilities of settlement of any or all issues, and if the matter is
not settled, to ensure that the matter is ready for the second stage which is a
formal hearing before another master. In other words, the preliminary hearings
for directions are essentially pre-trial hearings, and the masters conduct them
in a similar fashion to pre-trial hearings conducted by judges, adapting the
rules governing pre-trials to the exigencies of the masters’ court and the
particular reference.  For example, the masters generally regard anything said
during the pretrial to be privileged. This does not apply of course to
agreements made by the parties, statements of position by the parties on the
issues, directions for the disclosure of documents and anything to do with
procedural and disclosure issues.   The master issues a memorandum following
the pretrial. This memorandum is essentially intended to confirm agreements, to
outline the issues to be determined, to confirm any directions given during the
hearing and sometimes to give additional directions.

[
8
]

The first hearing for directions proceeded before me on November 6, 2007.  The petitioner was represented by counsel, T. Gutkin; the respondent
appeared without counsel.  At the outset of the hearing, I outlined the process
and then asked the parties to identify the outstanding issues to be determined
on the reference and to state his or her position with respect to same.

[
9
]

The respondent asked the court to make an order pursuant to Rule
55.02(5) that the petitioner’s father be added as a party.  This was opposed by
the petitioner. I advised the respondent that I was not prepared to make the
order requested, and noted that he was at liberty to pursue the matter through
a proper motion or an appeal as he saw fit. For additional clarification, I
noted in my memorandum issued with respect to this hearing, the following:

Rule
55.02(5) provides as follows:

Where
it appears to the master that any person ought to be added as a party to the
proceeding, the master may make an order adding the person as a defendant or
respondent and direct that the order, together with the order directing the
reference and a notice to party added on reference (Form 55B), be served on the
person, and on being served the person becomes a party to the proceeding.

The
rules provide that a master has the jurisdiction to add a person as a party to
the proceeding, but it certainly does not appear to me that anyone else ought
to be added as a party to this proceeding.  The reference here is very specific
to the three particular issues.  Moreover, the masters do not often add persons
as parties in non-family property act references and rarely do so in family
proceedings.  In my view, it would be the very rare case in which it would be
appropriate to add a third person as a party in a family property act
reference.  In any event, should a party believe a person should be added as a
party to a reference, the proper procedure is to file and serve a motion with
supporting material, including evidence and a motion brief, and a motion of
this nature would normally be set down for hearing on the masters’ uncontested
list for scheduling.

[
10
]

I would note that the respondent did not in fact subsequently
bring a motion to add the petitioner’s father as a party.

[
11
]

An issue also arose during the hearing concerning documents
presented by the parties which were not in English. It was agreed that a party
wishing to present such a document must also provide a translation of that
document into English prepared by a qualified independent translator.

[
12
]

The parties gave their positions on the petitioner’s pension. The
respondent’s position was that the pension was worth about $100,000.00 and that
he was entitled to a payment of half that amount plus interest from the date of
separation.

[
13
]

The petitioner’s position was that the value of the pension for
the purposes of sharing was $39,395.97 which was the amount that she received
when the pension was cashed out.  The petitioner took the position that all
contributions to the pension were made during married cohabitation and that
this entire amount was shareable.  Counsel for the petitioner gave the
respondent an envelope containing some documentation in Hebrew with respect to
the pension shortly before the hearing.

[
14
]

With respect to the pension, I issued the following directions:

1.

Mr. Kalo is to provide Mr. Gutkin
and the court with any documents regarding the pension upon which he wishes to
rely, together with translations where necessary, on or by December 15, 2007.

2.

Mr. Gutkin is to provide Mr. Kalo
with translations of the documents which he provided to Mr. Kalo prior to court
on or by
December 15, 2007
.

[
15
]

With respect to the jointly acquired household possessions, the
respondent’s position was that the total value of these items in the possession
of the petitioner was $50,000.00.

[
16
]

The petitioner’s position was that the total value of these items
was $675.00.  She provided a list of the jointly acquired items she alleges
were in the marital home as at the date of separation and the alleged values of
each item in her Summary of Assets and Liabilities.

[
17
]

I issued the following directions with respect to the household
items:

3.

Mr. Kalo is to provide Mr. Gutkin
and the court with a list of the jointly acquired household possessions that
were in the marital home as at the date of separation and the alleged values of
each item.

[
18
]

With respect to the wedding presents, the respondent’s position
was that the total value of wedding gifts in the petitioner’s possession was
$45,000.00. Included in this total, was $20,000.00 which he said was the value
of a vehicle which he alleged the parties received as a wedding gift and which
he alleged was sold to buy cars in use at the date of separation, and
$25,000.00 which was the value he attributes to other wedding gifts he alleged
that the parties received, including jewelry, art and silver dishes.

[
19
]

The petitioner’s position was that the value of the wedding gifts
for which she must account would be less than $15,000.00 but she was prepared
to stipulate that the wedding gifts had a value of $15,000.00 for the purpose
of the reference.

[
20
]

I issued the following directions with respect to the wedding
gifts:

4.

Mr. Kalo is to provide Mr. Gutkin
and the court with a list of the wedding presents he alleges the petitioner
retained as of the date of separation and the alleged values of each item.

5.

The petitioner is to provide Mr.
Kalo and the court with a list of the wedding presents she alleges she retained
as of the date of separation and the alleged values of each item.

[
21
]

In my memorandum issued after the hearing (Document  379), I
reminded the parties, as I had at the hearing, that a party who wishes to rely
on expert evidence at the formal hearing must provide and file a copy of the
expert’s report at the preliminary hearing for directions. I noted that Queen’s
Bench Rule 53.03, which deals with expert reports, applies with necessary
changes to the conduct of a reference, pursuant to Rule 55.02(13). Rule 53.03
reads as follows:

Service
of report

53.03(1)
A party who intends to call an expert witness at
trial shall include as part of the party’s pre-trial brief a copy of a report,
signed by the expert, setting out the expert’s name, address and
qualifications, and the substance of the proposed testimony.

Expert
called as witness

53.03(2)
The report is admissible in evidence but any party to
the action may serve notice in writing on the party tendering the report not less
than 10 days before the trial requiring the expert who prepared and signed the
report to be called as a witness and may cross-examine him or her on the
report; and it shall be the responsibility of the party tendering the report to
subpoena and pay for the attendance of the expert but the court may include the
cost of such subpoena and attendance as an item of taxable costs.

Admissibility

53.03(3)
Subject to section 50 of The Manitoba Evidence Act
(dealing with medical reports) no report is admissible in evidence and no
expert may testify, except with leave of the trial judge, unless subrule (1)
has been complied with.

[
22
]

The matter was adjourned to a date to be set. Shortly after the
hearing, the court received a letter from Mr. Gutkin advising that the
petitioner would be acting in person on the reference and a Notice of Intention
to Act in Person was subsequently filed by her (document 380).

Reference Order – Further Directions by Allen J.

[
23
]

Following this first hearing, in the course of preparing the memorandum
and reviewing the relevant documents in relation to it and considering certain
comments made during the hearing, I came to the conclusion that the master
needed further clarification or direction from the referring judge on several
issues. Accordingly, pursuant to
Rule 54.05(1), by letter
dated November 13, 2007, (document 381) I referred these issues to the judge. I
wrote to Mercier A.C.J., as Allen J. was then on study leave.

[
24
]

I requested clarification of the following aspects of the
reference order:

1.

Are all wedding presents to be
valued whether they are jointly acquired or not?

2.

Valuation date for the wedding
presents that are to be valued.

3.

Are all household items acquired
during married cohabitation to be valued whether one person acquired the item
or both did?

4.

Do the household items to be
valued include gifts and inheritances from third parties?  Or does it only
include items purchased by one or both of them?

5.

Valuation date for household
items.

6.

Is the reference to determine
whether a particular item is a joint item coming within the terms of the
reference?

[
25
]

In her letter in response, dated November 30, 2007, (document 397) Allen J. clarified the reference order as follows:

1.
As the judgment, at paragraph 163, says “wedding presents received by the
couple,” only jointly acquired wedding presents are to be valued.  If there is
a dispute about whether a particular wedding present was a present to the
couple or to one of the parties individually, the master will determine whether
an item is a joint item.

2.
The valuation date for all jointly owned property (wedding presents and
household items) will be the date the reference order was made - July 30, 2007.

3.
Only jointly owned household items are to be valued.  Again if there is a
dispute about whether an item was jointly purchased, the master will determine
that issue.

4.
As the pre-nuptial agreement was upheld, any property covered by that agreement
is not at issue on the reference. Therefore, the reference does not include
gifts and inheritances given to either party or any household property
purchased and paid for by either party where the source of the purchase was
from non-shareable funds.

5.
See 2 above.

6.
On the reference, the master will determine whether a particular item is a
joint item.

[
26
]

Copies of this letter were forwarded to the parties on December 4, 2007 (document 399).

Letter from respondent dated November 15, 2008 (Document
383)

[
27
]

Prior to receiving Allen J.’s letter, I received a letter from
the respondent (document 383) in which he asserted that my memorandum regarding
the November 6, 2007 hearing was in error because I had not referred to his
claim for the “
actual and specific
return of personal items, most of
which have great
sentimental value
, all belonging and relating to him,
and among those (but not only) the writer various
clothing items
.”  In
my response dated November 27, 2007, (document 393) I advised him, amongst
other things, that:

There
is clearly nothing in the reference order for the master to consider respecting
the “actual and specific return of personal items.”  This is a reference
pursuant to
The Family Property Act
.  That legislation does not provide
for return of any items.  It provides for a sharing of value.  In this case,
the only items which will be valued for the purpose of an equalization will be
the items set out in the reference order.

Second hearing for directions December 19, 2007

[
28
]

The second hearing for directions proceeded on December 19, 2007.  Both parties had filed material prior to the hearing.  The respondent
had filed a motion brief (document 395, filed November 29, 2007) and the
petitioner had filed two bound briefs containing the documents upon which she
intended to rely in the hearing of the reference: “Summary and Documents
Regarding the Petitioner’s Pension with Radview Software in Israel” (“the
petitioner’s pension brief”, document 405) and “Additional Documents Relied on
by the Petitioner on the Reference to the Master” (document 404).

[
29
]

The petitioner’s pension brief contained many documents detailing
the transactions surrounding the cash out of her pension and also translations
of the documents in Hebrew prepared by one Rachel Stockhammer. Documents
entitled “Certificate of Translation” were attached to each translation.   They
were dated December 6, 2007, and signed by Rachel Stockhammer who stated that
she was an “Atio Certified Translator”.  A seal on the certificates indicates
that “Atio” stands for the Association of Translators and Interpreters of
Ontario.

[
30
]

At the hearing, the respondent asserted that the translations
were inaccurate and that he wanted Ms Stockhammer to be called as a witness
pursuant to rule 53.03(1).  The court noted that this rule has nothing to do
with translation or interpretation, but commented that a party wishing to
tender a document which requires translation would in the ordinary course be
required to present the translator at the trial to satisfy the court that the
translator is qualified and the translation is accurate.  This of course is
only necessary if the opposite party is not prepared to accept the document.
Obviously if the court considers that the translator was required to be called
unnecessarily, there may be significant cost consequences.  The respondent
stated that he was obtaining his own translation of the documents and requested
an adjournment for that purpose.

[
31
]

I reviewed the parties’ compliance with the directions previously
given by me. The petitioner had complied fully with my directions. The
respondent had not.

[
32
]

The respondent had been directed to provide a list of the jointly
acquired household possessions that were in the marital home as at the date of
separation and the alleged values of each item. While in his brief he commented
on the household possessions, he did not provide the list he had been directed
to provide.

[
33
]

The respondent had been directed to provide a list of the wedding
presents he alleges the petitioner retained as of the date of separation and
the alleged values of each item.  While in his brief he commented on the
wedding presents, he did not provide the list he had been directed to provide.

[
34
]

The respondent had been directed to provide any documents
regarding the pension upon which he wanted to rely, together with translations
where necessary, on or by December 15, 2007.

[
35
]

The only document put forward by the respondent was a bank
statement pertaining to the petitioner’s personal account for the period ending
September 5, 2003, which statement includes a reference to a “credit memo” and
a “withdrawal” on August 20, 2003 of $99,000.00.  Accordingly, I told him that
this is the only document he will be permitted to tender at the formal hearing,
subject of course to the hearing master’s determination as to admissibility.

[
36
]

The parties were asked whether they intended to call any expert
witnesses. The respondent said that he didn’t know yet and he “might”. The
petitioner said that she would be calling D. Stevens of Gray’s Carter’s
Appraisals if necessary.  She had already included the appraisal in her
materials.

[
37
]

The parties were asked for a list of witnesses they intend to
call. The respondent listed the following individuals, in addition to himself:

Charles
Shore, Fanny Shore, Rolando Martin, Larry Saifer, Gail Asper, Arnold Freeman,
Sam Vickar, Sari Secter Blatt, Rachel Margolis, Jeff Shwaid, Marill Shwaid,
Romin Megid, Harvey Secter, Larry Frostiak, Aron Margolis, and Dave Blatt.
(phonetic)

[
38
]

He told the court that there may be others and that he reserved
the right to call others.  The petitioner said that she would testify and might
be calling her parents and Larry Frostiak if necessary.  In response to the
respondent’s request that she undertake to call her parents and Rolando Martin,
her common-law spouse, as witnesses, she stated that she would undertake to
make them available without the need for subpoenas but she would not undertake
to call them as witnesses herself.

[
39
]

The parties addressed the question of which party would proceed
first at the hearing.  The court directed that the respondent, as the
initiating party, would proceed first.

[
40
]

The parties were asked to estimate the time they believe should
be set aside for the hearing. The respondent stated two or three weeks. The
petitioner stated that it should take two or three days at most.

[
41
]

The court indicated to the parties that the length of time
estimated by the respondent was excessive in relation to the narrow issues to
be determined on the reference, and that the court was not willing to set the
matter down for a contested hearing without giving greater consideration to
this matter. The hearing was therefore adjourned
sine die
.  I advised
the parties that I would advise by letter of my decision in this respect.

[
42
]

I subsequently issued a memorandum respecting this hearing and
also wrote to the parties giving further directions as set out below.

My letter dated January 4, 2008 (Document 411)

[
43
]

By letter dated January 4, 2008, I advised the parties that I had
considered this and other related issues. I referred to the rules and pointed
out that it is the master’s responsibility to control the process and ensure
that court resources are used efficiently and that the parties are not
subjected to unnecessary time and expense.  I stated:

…a
reference of two to three weeks duration on a full accounting under
The
Family Property Act
would be most unusual. Given the very narrow issues
here referred to the master, the reference should take very little court time.
I am also concerned about Mr. Kalo’s general attitude toward these proceedings
in light of continued personal irrelevant comments and speeches disparaging Ms
Shore, her family and her friends, his failure to comply with the court’s
directions from the last hearing, and his comments as to the witnesses he intends
to call, amongst other things.

[
44
]

In the letter, amongst other things, I specifically issued the
following directions:

1.

By January 31, 2008, Mr. Kalo will
provide in writing:

•

a list of the material witnesses
he wishes to call,

•

a detailed explanation for each
witness of the evidence that he expects each of them to provide, and

•

an explanation of  why the
evidence of each is relevant.

This
document will be provided to Ms Shore and the court.

2.

By
January 31, 2008
, Mr. Kalo will
advise the court in writing, with a copy to Ms Shore, whether he intends to
call any expert witnesses. If so, he will identify his expert witnesses and
provide copies of their reports, in compliance with Queen’s Bench Rule 53.03.
Any expert report should have been provided in advance of the hearing for
directions before me.

[
45
]

I stated that I would review the respondent’s written submissions
and determine which witnesses he would be permitted to call at the formal
hearing and the number of days of court time that would be assigned for the
formal hearing. I directed that the respondent would be limited to those
witnesses.

The respondent’s submission dated January 11, 2008
(Document 415)

[
46
]

The respondent addressed the court by letter dated January 11, 2008 in which he took issue with my memorandum and the letter of January 4,
2008.  He objected to the statements in the memorandum that he had not complied
with my directions with respect to the jointly acquired property and wedding
present lists, and asserted that he had fully complied.  He asked for an
extension of the time limit to file additional materials to comply with the
directions in my January 4, 2008 letter because he said that he would be
writing his final law exam at the Law Society on January 31, 2008.

The respondent’s submission dated
February 4, 2008

(Document 426)

[
47
]

In this submission, the respondent dealt with the issue of the
witnesses that he intends to call at the hearing.  He advised that he had
decided to significantly reduce his witness list and to not call any experts.  He
stated that he intended to call only eight witnesses, in addition to himself:

Charles and
Fanny

Shore. He stated that they are the “petitioner’s wealthy parents. They are
the ones who held the wedding party at the time, and they were anyhow very
dominant in all financial aspects of the petitioner’s life all along the
marriage and separation.  Accordingly they can provide clear evidence as
to all the matters in dispute…” He estimated that Mr. Shore’s examination
would take one hour and Mrs. Shore’s testimony would take half an hour.

Rolando Martin: He stated
that “the writer met with Mr. Martin a few times in the past and the
issue, that the witness is well familiar with, of the household
possessions (including personal belongings) owned by the parties (all held
so far by the petitioner in her home), was discussed with him in length at
those meetings (as a way of an indirect communication with the petitioner
in order to resolve the dispute amicably).  Thus, this witness is called
to provide evidence as to this issue.”  He estimated that Mr. Martin’s
examination would take a half hour.

Arnold
Freiman: He stated that “This witness, a friend
and neighbor of the petitioner’s parents, is the owner of a big local
store known as ‘Advance Electronics’.  When the parties arrived to
Canada
and
shortly before the separation they purchased together, from the witness
himself and at his store, a wide set of expensive electric products (the
ones brought to
Canada
could have not been used due to a different
power system).  All those items are held by the petitioner in her home
since the separation.  The witness is to provide detailed evidence,
support by invoices, as to the value (including current) of all that had
been purchased at his store by the parties.”  He estimated that Mr.

Decision

[
66
]

Queen’s Bench Rule 55.01(1) gives the master wide discretion in
the procedure to be used on a reference. It reads:

55.01(1)    A
master shall, subject to any directions contained in the order directing the
reference, devise and adopt the
simplest, least expensive and most expeditious
manner
of conducting the reference and may,

(a) give
such directions as are necessary; and

(b)
dispense
with any procedure ordinarily taken that the master considers to be
unnecessary, or adopt a procedure different from that ordinarily taken
. (Emphasis
added)

[
67
]

Queen’s Bench Rule 55.02(3)
gives the
master the authority to give directions as to the evidence that is to be
received. It reads:

At
the hearing for directions, the master shall give such directions for the
conduct of the reference as are just, including,

(a) the
time and place at which the reference is to proceed;

(b) any
special directions concerning the parties who are to attend; and

(c) any
special directions concerning what evidence is to be received and how documents
are to be proved.

[
68
]

The directions given by the master in a reference at any stage
are orders of the court and bind the parties.  Rule 55.02(11) provides that
“the directions need not be embodied in a formal order or
report to bind the parties.”

[
69
]

In the course of this hearing, I have given clear directions to
the respondent to provide information on the household items and the wedding
presents in order to delineate the issues and focus the formal hearing on the
extremely narrow issues referred to the master by Allen J.

[
70
]

The respondent has refused to comply with my directions regarding
the lists.  As far as I can tell, the respondent’s position on the disclosure
issue seems to be that he is unable to provide anything more specific because
the petitioner remained in the home and retained all the parties’ possessions,
and he intends to prove his case by subpoenaing witnesses and documents and by
cross-examination of the petitioner and the other witnesses.

[
71
]

For the reasons cited by the petitioner, I cannot imagine that
anything of any significant probative value could result from the testimony of
Messrs Martin and Saifer, whom he still intends to call. In any event, his
free-wheeling fishing-expedition approach to the litigation is totally
impractical, and contrary to the policy of the court and the rules to encourage
full and meaningful disclosure prior to the trial of the issues. It is a waste
of everyone’s time, abusive of the process, and clearly unfair to the
petitioner who has been completely cooperative in this reference.  The hearing
before the master is not an examination for discovery. If the respondent wished
to examine for discovery, he should have done it some time ago. I would note
that it appears in fact that examinations for discovery were conducted prior to
the trial before Allen J. and property issues were canvassed. (See document
358).

[
72
]

I have a clear duty “to devise and adopt the
simplest, least
expensive and most expeditious manner
of conducting the reference”.  The
respondent has made that impossible.     Given the respondent’s intransigence,
what are my options to achieve this? The master has no power of contempt to
enforce compliance with its directions, or indeed appropriate conduct in the
court room.

[
73
]

The respondent seems to be impervious to cost orders and indeed
indicated to me in the hearing on December 19,

2007, that the bigger
the costs, the bigger the bankruptcy. Making the continuation of the reference
to a formal hearing contingent on the payment of costs he almost certainly will
not pay is unfair to the petitioner as it leaves the matter unresolved.

[
74
]

The petitioner has urged that I dismiss the respondent’s claims.
I hesitated to take this unusual step because this first stage of the
procedures established by the masters on these references, as explained above,
is a “pre-trial”. I advised the parties at the outset, as I always do, of the
nature of the hearing. In particular, I noted that because of the settlement
goal, I would not be making the final determination as to the substantive
issues, any comments in relation to settlement made to me during this process
were confidential, and I would not share any comments of this nature with the
master hearing the matter.

[
75
]

However, in these particular circumstances, on reflection I do
not think this is a problem. The masters’ preliminary hearings in family
property matters are very similar to case conferences in family proceedings.
Rule 70.24(30) provides that discussions at a case conference are without
prejudice and shall not be referred to in motions or at the trial or hearing of
the proceeding, except as disclosed in the judge’s memorandum. Rule 70.24(27)
sets out the kind of information that can be set out in the memorandum and it
is restricted to orders, directions, matters resolved, outstanding issues, and
so forth, in other words the same kinds of things that are set out in the
masters’ memoranda.  Most significantly, rule 70.24 (25) permits a case
conference judge, where a party has failed to follow the rules,  to make any
order the judge considers appropriate, including striking out all or part of a
party’s pleadings.  Given the wide discretion given to the master in the
conduct of the reference, in my view the master has the discretion to make a
determination of the matters referred to the master at any stage if the master
considers it appropriate to do so.

[
76
]

In this case, I am satisfied that I have no obligation to refer
this matter to a formal hearing before another master.  I believe the only
reasonable approach is to short-circuit the normal reference process
established by the masters, and issue a report at this stage without proceeding
to a formal hearing before a different master.  I do not believe there is a
real problem, as I am not taking into account, or referring to, any “without
prejudice” comments made by the parties to me respecting settlement. In my
view, to continue with the formal hearing would be an abuse of process. I
believe the respondent, through his behaviour, has forfeited any right he may
have to proceed to a formal hearing. Furthermore, in my view, the only credible
evidence that could be put before another master in a formal hearing, is that
of the petitioner, based on her documentary disclosure, and the appraisal she
has submitted. Based on the evidence that will likely be put before the master,
it is difficult to conceive of the master coming to any other conclusion.

[
77
]

[
78

[
79

[
80

He has presented to me no documentary evidence which would

[
81

[
82
]

With respect to the other items, the respondent has not provided

[
83
]

I will now turn to his claim to

one half of the jointly
acquired household possessions.

As noted previously, the only items to
be valued are those that were in the marital home on the date the parties
separated (March 9, 2003), and they are to be valued as of July 30, 2007.

[
84
]

[
85

The respondent’s submission is contained in his March brief
(document 450). He claims that the total value of the household items is at
least $50,000.00 and consists of: p
ossessions
that the parties packed  and shipped to Winnipeg (to which he ascribes a total
value of $35,000.00); possessions that the parties carried with them when
entering Canada (a video camera, a digital camera, a “standard plus zoom”
camera, two mobile computers, silver, gold and diamond jewellery; four

condition”, “mobile hitter”, dishwasher, electric stove, two vacuum cleaners
(to which he ascribes a total value of $5000.00); and other Items which he says
that the parties purchased in Winnipeg, “such as”: three televisions, a
surround system,  two CD players, a VCR, two vacuum cleaners, and a desk
computer (to which he ascribes a total value of $5000.00).

[
86
]

The respondent’s only documentary evidence of the items shipped
to Canada is the two lists attached to his November 29, 2007 brief.  The first
list is entitled “insurance form”, and includes a “packing list”. It lists a
number of items or categories of items. There is no indication of value. The
second document lists a number of items or categories of items with some
notations of quantities and round figures as to “price per unit”.  I understand
these documents were prepared at the time of the parties’ moving from Israel to
Winnipeg in 2002.   It also appears that both lists may relate to the same
items.

[
87
]

These lists are of extremely little evidentiary value. The
valuation date is July 30, 2007, not 2002. “Price per unit” is not the same
thing as “fair market value”.  There is no information how “price per unit” was
determined or by whom or for what purpose. They are not appraisals by qualified
appraisers. Both lists include clothing which is not included in a family
property act accounting.  The only items that were to be included in the
accounting are those items that were in the marital home at the date of
separation (March 9, 2003).

[
88
]

At the most they give some indication of the quantity and type of
household items that probably ended up in the family home a few months later.
The petitioner submits that most of the items in the list are not shareable as
they were acquired by her prior to the marriage by gift or inheritance, or
purchased by her prior to the marriage.

[
89
]

For example, she notes that there were additional items in the

[
90
]

Regarding the items the respondent claims that the parties
carried with them when entering Canada (cameras, mobile computers, jewelry and
watches), he has produced no documentation whatsoever to substantiate this
allegation. The petitioner commented in her brief (document 404): that the only
cameras brought to Canada were an Olympus camera which was given to the
respondent after the separation and a video camera borrowed from her father:
that she did not have a mobile computer when she came to Canada; and that all
the jewelry she had when she came to Canada was either pre-acquired, gifts or
inheritances and not jointly acquired. She admits she had a Cartier watch when
they separated but says she paid for this watch and it was not jointly
acquired.

[
91
]

Regarding the respondent’s claim that there were shareable items
left at the marital home in Israel for the temporary use of the tenant,
including carpets, furniture, etc., the respondent has not produced any
documentation substantiating the existence of these items, their value, or
whether in fact they were left temporarily. The petitioner says that many of
the items never existed, and those items that were left in the home were for
the use of the tenants, who eventually purchased the home, and these items were
included in the purchase price.  In any event, they are irrelevant because the
marital home at the date of separation was in Winnipeg, not Israel.

[
92
]

Respecting the electronic items which he claims the parties
purchased in Winnipeg before the separation (televisions, etc.), again he has
produced no evidence whatsoever to support his claims.  He did attach to his
brief what he says is a photo of a desk top computer in the petitioner’s home.
However, the petitioner explains that computer belongs to her current employer.
She says that she did bring a desk top computer to Winnipeg but this computer
was owned by her former employer, Radview Software, and was returned to that
company when her employment with it ended.

[
93
]

The petitioner says that the only television acquired jointly by
them after coming to Canada was the Sharp set for which she is accounting. She
says the parties did not acquire a surround sound system then and did not have
one at the date of separation. She says that they did not purchase CD players
after arriving in Canada and the only VCR in the home at separation was
acquired by her prior to marriage.  She says her father gave her a vacuum
cleaner when they came to Canada.  Perhaps I should point out that I mention
the petitioner’s explanations of this and other items not as evidence currently
before the court, but as an indication of the credibility of the evidence that
she intends to adduce should the matter have proceeded to a formal hearing, as
opposed to that which could be expected of the respondent’s evidence, given his
explanations and claims.

[
94
]

With respect to the household items for which the petitioner
agrees to account, the respondent has not provided the court with an appraisal
disputing the petitioner’s valuation, and he is now precluded from doing so.

[
95
]

With respect to the respondent’s claim to the petitioner’s
pension with her Israeli employer Radview Software that was accrued between the
date of the marriage of the parties and the date of their separation, the
petitioner has presented extensive documentation supporting a value of
$35,956.21.  The documents are contained in the petitioner’s pension brief
(document 405). Her pension brief includes documents in Hebrew regarding the
pension funds, and translations of those documents by Ms Stockhammer. The
petitioner has also filed an affidavit by Ms Stockhammer (document 423)  in
which Ms Stockhammer deposes that she is a certified translator through the
Association of Translators and Interpreters of Ontario, that she is well
acquainted with both English and Hebrew, and that her translations of the
various documents are accurate.  The petitioner explains that she had to go out
of the province to find a translator willing to become involved in this matter.

[
96
]

The petitioner contributed to this pension while in Israel.  She
cashed out the pension after the parties separated.  She retained a law firm in
Israel to assist her in cashing out the pension. She says that the pension
funds she ultimately received came from four different plans, and were paid to
the law firm at four different times. Tab 1 to her pension brief is a statement
from the law firm summarizing the amounts received, and when they were
received, the total amount being $29,244.58 US. The petitioner states this
amount was transferred to her on December 26, 2004, the date of the statement.
The value in Canadian currency as of that date was $35,956.21.  This amount is
net of charges by the law firm for its services.  I would note that this amount
differs from the value of $39,395.97 that the petitioner originally asserted in
her Summary of Assets and Liabilities.  The difference appears to relate to the
increase in value of the Canadian dollar against the U.S. dollar.  The lower
value reflects the value in Canadian funds of the amount she received at the
time she received the funds. Her position that this is the amount that is
shareable is reasonable given the nature of this asset and the documentation
that she has provided.

[
97
]

While the respondent asserts that the value of the pension is
“about” $100,000.00 (see document 395), he has disclosed no evidence that would
support this assertion.  The only document produced by him upon which he says
he is relying is a Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce statement regarding the
petitioner’s personal account for the month ending September 5, 2003.  This statement shows a “credit memo” on August 29, 2003 for $99,990.00 and a “withdrawal”
of $99,990.00 on the same date.  The respondent’s position seems to be that
this reflects a deposit of this amount by the petitioner and he asserts that
this is related to her pension. The petitioner presents a perfectly credible
explanation: this is a bank error and does not reflect a deposit by her of this
amount.  In any event, the respondent has not disclosed an iota of evidence
linking this amount to her pension in any manner whatsoever.

[
98
]

The respondent appears to be of the view that he can somehow
diminish the value of the petitioner’s documentary evidence regarding the
pension funds because he alleges the translations she has provided of those
documents that are in Hebrew are somehow in error.  He has insisted that the
petitioner produce the translator as a witness at the hearing so that he can
cross-examine her about her translations.  He has produced no translations of his
own of the petitioner’s documents.  He has not even specified the alleged
errors in the translations. In the circumstances, I consider his position on
this simply frivolous.  Accordingly, in my view, the only credible evidence on
this issue is that of the petitioner.

[
99
]

An additional factor underscoring the inability of the master to
continue with this reference is the respondent’s conduct throughout the
reference process.  While comments made during this stage of the reference are
generally, as explained above, privileged, and the parties should feel they can
speak freely, this freedom does not give the parties’
carte blanche
to
indulge in scandalous, frivolous, vexatious and abusive comments. During the
hearings, the respondent continually interrupted the master, was often
unresponsive to her questions, argumentative, bombastic and engaged in
irrelevant and inflammatory oratory, the latter for the most part being
frequent irrelevant personal comments apparently intended to disparage the
petitioner, her family, her friends and her community.  Despite my warnings to
the respondent that such comments would not be tolerated, he continued to make
them.

[
100
]

For
example, in my letter to the parties dated January 4, 2008, I stated that I
continued to be concerned with the issue of respect for the court and
appropriate conduct in the courtroom, and I directed that the respondent
henceforward desist from making any “editorial” comments, or any comments of a
personal and totally irrelevant nature with regard to the petitioner, her
family or her friends.

[
101
]

In
his submission dated January 11, 2008, the petitioner, in objecting to this
comment, continued in the same vein. He stated:

The
respondent was surprised to find a large and somehow angry reference, at the
letter to the parties, as to certain comments that he might have made here and
there.

The
respondent trusts that these comments, which subject matter is apparently the
proved strength of the local Jewish community as well as its obvious strong
ties to the legal system, would not be taken out of context and would not be
blown out of proportions.

After
all, the matters heard now by the court are emotionally charged and crucial for
the self-represented and non-fluent respondent, who is conducting a long-time
“up the hill” bitter family dispute.

This
dispute, as well known to the court by now, goes back to the sophisticated
abduction of the respondent’s two beloved young daughters from the Middle East
to
Winnipeg
, together with the brutal and sudden take over of all that the
respondent ever gained.

Moreover,
the petitioner – who forced this dispute upon the respondent – is, as was
determined by the honorable trial Judge, the daughter of a very rich Jewish
family, and as such is enjoying the support of many Jewish local entities,
among them the Asper community center, which choose to keep on intervening in
the (otherwise private) dispute due to the influence of petitioner’s family.

[
102
]

I
again admonished him on this topic in my letter dated March 5, 2008, and commented that this is a matter for costs. I stated:

In
Mr. Kalo’s letter dated January 11, 2008, he appears to be taking objection to
my direction that he must henceforward desist from making irrelevant comments
about the petitioner, her family and/or her friends. He then proceeds to make
several of those very comments. This may be a matter that may be addressed in
costs.

[
103
]

I
would note that, while his refusal to desist in these comments fortifies me in
my decision that a formal hearing before the master would be an abuse of the
court, it is not a reason on which I have based my decision to issue a report
at this time.

[
104
]

In
reporting on this reference to the judge, it is my obligation to make findings
on the matters referred to me.  Based on the only credible and relevant evidence
before me, my findings are as follows:

The respondent’s claim to one half of the jointly
acquired wedding presents received by the parties that were retained by
the petitioner on the date the parties separated (March 9, 2003), valued
as of July 30, 2007.
I accept the petitioner’s position that the
shareable value of these items is $3500.00.  The respondent is therefore
entitled to one-half of that amount or $1750.00.

The respondent’s claim to one half of the jointly
acquired household possessions of the parties that were in the marital
home  on the date the parties separated (March 9, 2003), valued as of July
30, 2007.
I accept the petitioner’s position that the shareable
value of these items is $480.00.  The respondent is therefore entitled to
one half of that amount or $240.00.

The respondent’s claim to that portion of the
petitioner’s pension with her Israeli employer Radview Software that was
accrued between the date of the marriage of the parties and the date of
their separation.
I accept the petitioner’s position that the
shareable value of this item is $35,956.21.  The respondent is therefore
entitled to one half of that amount or $17,978.10.

Costs

[
105
]

The
respondent’s refusal to comply with my directions, without considering any
other factor, justifies an award of costs against him for this reference.  I
recognize that the petitioner has been for the most part self-represented in
this reference. There will be costs to the petitioner of $800.00 plus
reasonable disbursements. The petitioner may submit a bill of costs

respecting the disbursements, supported by receipts.  If she submits a bill of
costs, she will forward a copy of same to the respondent who may then submit
any objections by letter to the court.

J.
M. Cooper
